Their constancy follows explicitly from the prose, while their state-space typing is inherited from q. [Printed page 5, 'piecewise constant' and (1.11); printed page 1, q : R × R → R^m.]

For every x < 0, q(x,0) = q_l; for every x > 0, q(x,0) = q_r. The universal scope is expressed by the cases of the displayed function specification. [Printed page 5, (1.11).]
conclusions: A hyperbolic equation together with these special initial data is what the passage calls a Riemann problem. This is a definition of a problem, rather than an existence or uniqueness theorem for its solution. [Printed page 5, Section 1.2.1, opening paragraph and (1.11).]

The source does not require those eigenvalues to be distinct. [Printed page 1, (1.1); printed page 3, opening definition of hyperbolicity.]

The finite-volume choices q_l = Q_{i−1} and q_r = Q_i instantiate the definition using neighboring cell averages; they do not occur as restrictions in its opening paragraph. [Printed page 5, Section 1.2.1, opening paragraph and paragraph following (1.11).]

contract_plain_english: A Riemann problem is a hyperbolic equation equipped with initial data that are constant on each side of one spatial point. Choosing that point as zero, the source prescribes q(x,0) = q_l for every x < 0 and q(x,0) = q_r for every x > 0, leaving the value at zero unspecified. The prose calls the separation a single jump discontinuity, but the displayed formula does not explicitly exclude equal states. [Printed page 5, Section 1.2.1 and (1.11).] The inherited setting includes scalar and real vector-valued first-order systems. [Printed pages 1 and 3, discussion of (1.1) and first-order hyperbolic systems.] The subsequent use of neighboring cell averages is an application, and the similarity-solution description is qualified by 'typically'; neither adds an unconditional defining requirement. [Printed page 5, paragraph following (1.11).]
